title: How to seal the back of a cross-stitch piece
subtitle: Securing loose thread ends on the reverse so they cannot pull through
excerpt: Sealing the back of a finished cross-stitch piece means checking every thread end is woven in and trimmed, then optionally applying a thin layer of fabric stiffener or adhesive to anchor the back permanently. This is the final step before mounting or gifting a piece that will see regular handling.
sourceNotes: Cross-stitch back sealing and finishing. Standard guidance in major cross-stitch publisher guides.

glossaryTerms.definition: The six-strand embroidery thread used for cross-stitch.
A stiff, evenly-woven cross-stitch fabric with clearly visible squares formed by groups of threads.

content.text: ends are woven in and trimmed to under 5 mm, and optionally a thin layer of diluted fabric stiffener is applied to the back of the
to fix everything in place. The adhesive layer is optional for framed pieces but useful for pieces that will be handled frequently, such as book covers or cushion backs.

Lay the finished piece face down on a clean, flat surface. Using a magnifying glass if needed, check every thread end. Each end should be woven under at least four adjacent thread runs and trimmed to within 5 mm of the last weave point.

Trim any tails longer than 5 mm with sharp embroidery scissors. Cut close to the last weave point but not so close that the end has no anchor. The cut end should sit flat against the fabric and not stand up.

For framed pieces, this is sufficient finishing. Check from the front that no thread tails are visible through the Aida holes; a dark tail behind a pale fabric can show through. If any are visible, trim them shorter or push them further under adjacent runs.

For pieces that will be handled: mix a thin solution of PVA glue (white craft glue) with water, approximately one part glue to three parts water. Paint a thin layer across the back of the stitched area with a flat brush. Do not allow it to soak through to the front.

Pin the piece out flat on a blocking board and allow the PVA layer to dry completely before removing the pins. The dry layer should be firm but not stiff, and the piece should lie flat and square. The thread ends are now fixed in place and secure.

items.symptom: The PVA glue soaked through to the front and stiffened the fabric surface
items.cause: The glue solution was too concentrated or was applied too heavily.
items.fix: Dilute the glue further and apply a thinner layer next time. For the current piece, dampen the front with clean water to soften the glue, allow it to relax, and press from the front with a damp cloth to restore the fabric hand. A very stiff front may need to be framed rather than used as a soft finishing.

items.symptom: Thread ends are still visible from the front after sealing
items.cause: The tails were not trimmed short enough, or they are sitting in Aida holes rather than behind thread runs.
items.fix: Before sealing, push each tail under a thread run with the tip of a tapestry needle rather than leaving it to lie across an open hole. After sealing, a tail visible through a hole can be carefully cut shorter with small scissors from the back.

content.text: Sealing the back with PVA is particularly useful for cross-stitch applied to items that will be washed or handled frequently. The dilute PVA is water-soluble when wet; it holds the threads in place during normal use but can be removed if the piece needs to be unpicked and reworked.
